nameStory: This tiny amphipod carries the name of French naturalist Jean Baptiste Bory de Saint-Vincent, whose middle name was Prévost. Like many scientific discoveries of the 1800s, this little crustacean was named to honor the researchers who helped expand our understanding of marine life.
description: Apohyale prevostii is a small marine amphipod, a type of sideways-swimming crustacean that looks like a tiny shrimp curved into a C-shape. These translucent creatures are typically only 3-8 millimeters long (about the size of a grain of rice) and have segmented bodies with multiple pairs of legs. They're part of the beach flea family, though they spend most of their time in shallow marine waters rather than hopping on beaches. Their bodies are laterally compressed, meaning they're flattened from side to side like a fish.

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Distinctive C-curved, laterally flattened body that feels firm but slightly squishy when gently pressed, like a small piece of cooked rice

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny at 3-8mm long, easily fitting on your pinky fingernail with room to spare

idTips.label: Swimming pattern
idTips.description: Swims on its side with jerky, darting movements rather than the smooth gliding of small fish

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of thread-like antennae that constantly twitch and probe the water, feeling delicate as spider silk if touched

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Seven pairs of legs visible along the underside, some paddle-like for swimming, others claw-like for grasping

habitat: Found in shallow coastal waters along New England's rocky shores and tide pools, particularly in areas with good water circulation. They prefer areas with seaweed and algae where they can find food and shelter, typically in depths from the intertidal zone down to about 30 feet.

seasonality.spring: Active as waters warm, often found in shallow tide pools during low tide exploration. Look for their jerky swimming movements in clear water.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easiest to spot during peak warming. Often seen in large numbers in protected coves and among seaweed beds.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper water. Can be found during low tide investigations of rocky areas.
seasonality.winter: Less active in cold water but still present. May require closer examination of tide pools and shallow areas during warmer winter days.

funFact: These tiny amphipods can jump completely out of the water when startled, launching themselves like microscopic dolphins despite having no fins - they use their powerful tail and legs to catapult through the surface tension.
confusionNotes: Often confused with small mysid shrimp or copepods, but amphipods swim on their side while mysids swim upright, and copepods have a more teardrop-shaped body. Remember: 'Amphipods flip on their side, mysids swim with pride.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'beach fleas,' most amphipods like this species are truly marine creatures that rarely venture onto actual beaches. The 'flea' name comes from their ability to jump and their small size, not their habitat preferences.
compareHints: Since this is the only Apohyale species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other hyalid amphipods by looking for its relatively robust build and active swimming behavior. Other similar amphipods in the region tend to be either much smaller and more delicate, or larger with more pronounced body segments.
